# Plain Language Terms

When a question asks the user for one of these items, write the explanation below **word for word**, right after the term. Do this the first time the term comes up in a session, and again whenever the user seems unsure. Do not substitute other definitions. For a technical term not in this table, give a one sentence plain explanation in the same style. The plan's glossary appendix uses the same wording.

| Term | Explanation to give the user |
|---|---|
| Business Continuity Plan (BCP) | A step by step playbook for keeping the most important parts of the business running when something suddenly goes wrong, and for getting back to normal afterwards. |
| Critical Business Function (CBF) | An activity the business cannot stop for long without serious harm, such as taking customer orders, paying staff or running a key system. If it stopped, customers, income, safety or legal duties would quickly suffer. |
| Business Impact Analysis (BIA) | A short review of what would hurt, how badly and how quickly if each activity stopped. It tells us which activities are critical and how fast they must be back. |
| Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption (MTPD) | The longest an activity can be stopped before the damage becomes unacceptable or hard to undo, for example customers leaving for good or a legal deadline being missed. |
| Recovery Time Objective (RTO) | The target time to get an activity working again, at least at a basic level. It must be shorter than the Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption, so there is a safety margin. |
| Recovery Point Objective (RPO) | How much recent data the business could afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of 1 hour means losing up to the last hour of data is acceptable, so backups must run at least every hour. |
| Minimum service level | The reduced level an activity must still deliver during the disruption, for example urgent orders only, taken by phone, up to 50 a day. |
| Dependencies | The people, systems, equipment, suppliers, buildings and records an activity needs in order to run. |
| Crisis Management Team (CMT) | The small group of people who take charge when the plan is activated. They make the decisions, direct the response and speak for the business. |
| Alternate | The back-up person for a role, who steps in if the main person is unavailable. |
| Alternate site | Somewhere else to work from if the usual premises cannot be used, such as staff homes, another office or a partner's premises. |
| Activation trigger | The event or warning sign that tells us to start using the plan, for example a fire alarm that leads to evacuation, or a key system being down for more than 30 minutes. |
| Severity level | A simple scale for how serious the situation is. It decides how much of the plan is used and who must be involved. |
| Call tree | A pre-agreed list of who calls whom, so everyone who needs to know is reached quickly, even if the usual systems are down. |
| Workaround | A temporary way of doing an activity when the usual way is not available, such as taking orders on paper while the system is down. |
| Vital records | Documents and data the business cannot operate or recover without, such as contracts, customer lists, insurance policies and passwords. |
| Holding statement | A short, pre-approved message saying what is known, what is being done and when the next update will come, used before all the facts are clear. |
| Stand-down | The formal decision that the emergency response is over and the business can move on to recovery or back to normal. |
| Tabletop exercise | A practice session where the team talks through a pretend incident step by step, to check that the plan works and everyone knows their part. |
| Key Risk Indicator (KRI) | A number tracked regularly that warns when a risk is getting closer to happening, for example the number of failed log-in attempts each day. |

Example question: "Which activities are your Critical Business Functions? A Critical Business Function is an activity the business cannot stop for long without serious harm, such as taking customer orders, paying staff or running a key system. If it stopped, customers, income, safety or legal duties would quickly suffer."
